questions.q: In Plucker's discharge tube, the glass at the anode (positive end) glowed with a pale green light, an effect called fluorescence. What did experimenters conclude about where the invisible rays causing this glow came from?
options: They originated at the negative electrode, or cathode, of the vacuum tube
They originated at the positive anode and travelled back toward the cathode
They were produced in the glass itself where it glowed green
They came from the high-voltage induction coil outside the tube
questions.explanation: Although the glow appeared at the anode end, whatever caused it must have originated at the negative electrode, or cathode. Goldstein named these rays 'cathode rays' for exactly this reason, and the tubes became known as cathode ray tubes or discharge tubes.

questions.q: Why must a discharge tube be evacuated to a low gas pressure for cathode rays to be produced effectively?
options: At low pressure the glass fluoresces more brightly green
At low pressures, electrons can accelerate to faster speeds before colliding with gas particles
Low pressure increases the voltage delivered by the induction coil
Removing the gas stops the cathode from being negatively charged
questions.explanation: At low pressures the gas particles are spread far apart, so electrons leaving the cathode can accelerate to faster, higher speeds before colliding with gas particles. At higher pressure they would collide almost immediately and lose their energy before crossing the tube.

questions.q: Two parallel plates are separated by 5.0 cm and a potential difference of 200 V is applied across them, producing a uniform electric field. Calculate the strength of the electric field between the plates.
working: A force on a charge in this field would be \(F = qE\); for an electron, \(F = (1.6\times10^{-19})(4000) = 6.4\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{N}\) directed toward the positive plate.
questions.explanation: A uniform field between parallel plates is given by E = V/d. These are the plates used by Thomson and Millikan to study small charged particles; once E is known, the force on any charge follows from F = qE.

questions.q: An electron of charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C moves at 2.5 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a magnetic field of strength 2.0 × 10⁻² T. Calculate the magnitude of the magnetic force on the electron and state the shape of its path.
working: The path is circular, because the magnetic force always acts perpendicular to the velocity of the electron, providing a centripetal force.
questions.explanation: Apply F = qvB with sin 90° = 1. The path is circular because the force stays perpendicular to the velocity, so it acts as a centripetal force and bends the electron into a circle — stating why the path is circular is itself a mark.

questions.q: In Thomson's experiment the cathode rays passed between parallel plates connected to a battery. The rays moved toward the positively charged plate. What did this show about the rays?
options: The rays carried no charge and simply drifted toward the plate
The rays behaved as positive charges
The rays behaved as negative charges
The rays were a form of light bent by the plates
questions.explanation: Because the cathode rays were deflected toward the positively charged plate, and opposite charges attract, the rays must behave as negative charges. This deflection of cathode rays by an electric field was a cornerstone of Thomson's identification of the electron.

questions.q: Several observations of cathode rays were historically taken to fit the WAVE model rather than the particle model. Which of the following was one of those wave-model observations?
options: They could pass through thin metal foils without damaging them
Small paddlewheels turned when placed in the path of the rays
They were clearly deflected by magnetic fields
They travelled considerably more slowly than light
questions.explanation: Travelling in straight lines, casting shadows, and passing through thin metal foils all looked wave-like. Turning a paddlewheel, deflection by a magnetic field, and travelling more slowly than light fitted the particle model. The debate was resolved in 1897 when Thomson showed the rays were streams of negatively charged particles.

questions.q: From memory: early cathode rays appeared NOT to deflect in an electric field, which seemed to support the wave model. Explain why this absence of deflection was misleading and how Thomson resolved it.
keyPoints: The absence of electric-field deflection was the main restriction on the charged-particle theory at the time.

Within the imperfectly evacuated tube, the cathode rays ionised the residual gas; the ions were attracted to the plate of opposite charge and lined up, effectively neutralising the charge on the plates and cancelling the field.

Thomson improved the vacuum (higher exhaustion), removing the residual gas; the field was no longer neutralised and the beam deflected toward the positive plate, confirming the rays carry negative charge.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that the residual gas was ionised and the resulting ions neutralised the plates, and that a better vacuum revealed the true deflection toward positive, grade yourself Good or Easy. The key point is to blame the apparatus (poor vacuum), not a real property of the rays.

questions.q: Name the four classic cathode-ray observations (Cross, Paddle, Electric, Magnetic) and state the single conclusion each one supports.
keyPoints: Maltese cross: a sharp shadow forms on the fluorescent glass, so the rays travel in straight lines and are blocked by solid objects.
Paddle wheel: it rolls away from the cathode doing work against friction and gravity, so the rays carry momentum and energy — evidence of mass.
Electric field: the beam deflects toward the positive plate, so the rays carry negative charge.
Magnetic field: the beam curves like a negative charge would; this shows the rays are charged and moving, and since light is not deflected by a magnet, they are not simply light.
questions.explanation: If you got all four observations tied to their correct conclusion (straight lines, mass, negative charge, charged-and-moving/not-light), grade Good or Easy. If you missed one, that is the one to drill — write 'Cross, Paddle, Electric, Magnetic' first thing in the exam.

questions.q: A light paddle wheel placed in the path of cathode rays rolls along its rails away from the cathode, even slightly uphill. In the syllabus interpretation, what does this demonstrate?
options: The rays heat the gas, which pushes the wheel — proving nothing about the rays
The rays carry momentum and energy and can do mechanical work, evidence they are particles with mass
The rays carry negative charge, since the wheel moves
The rays are a wave, because waves transfer energy
questions.explanation: To roll a wheel and do mechanical work against friction and gravity, the rays must deliver momentum and kinetic energy — something a massless wave cannot do. So the paddle wheel is evidence the rays are particles possessing mass. (Modern analysis notes a heating/radiometer effect, but the mark-earning HSC interpretation is momentum transfer.)

questions.q: Analyse how observations of cathode rays in a discharge tube provide evidence that cathode rays consist of particles with both mass and charge. (6 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: When a light paddle wheel was placed in the path of the cathode rays, it rolled along its rails away from the cathode, even up a slight incline against friction and gravity. Because the rays transferred momentum and did mechanical work on the wheel, they must carry kinetic energy and momentum, which is evidence that cathode rays are particles possessing mass rather than a massless electromagnetic wave. When the rays passed between two charged parallel plates, the beam deflected toward the positively charged plate; since only a negative charge is attracted toward a positive plate, this shows cathode rays carry negative electric charge. This was confirmed when a magnetic field was applied: the beam followed a curved, circular path in the direction predicted for a negatively charged moving particle, again showing the rays are charged and in motion — and since light is not deflected by a magnet, this also shows they are not simply light. Supporting these conclusions, a Maltese cross cast a sharp shadow on the fluorescent glass, showing the rays travel in straight lines and are blocked by a solid object. Taken together, the paddle wheel provides evidence of mass and momentum, while the electric- and magnetic-field deflections provide evidence of negative charge, so cathode rays are streams of fast-moving, negatively charged particles with mass — the particles we now call electrons.

criteria.descriptor: Uses the paddle wheel (momentum, work, energy) to argue the rays have mass, contrasting with a massless wave.
Uses electric-field deflection toward the positive plate AND magnetic-field deflection to establish the rays carry negative charge and are moving.
Includes a supporting observation (Maltese cross shadow / straight-line travel) and/or that a magnet does not deflect light.
Synthesises the observations into the conclusion that cathode rays are negatively charged particles with mass (electrons).

questions.explanation: A full-mark six-marker links at least three observations to their conclusions (observation, reasoning, conclusion) and then synthesises them: paddle wheel for mass; electric and magnetic deflection for negative charge.
